title: Integrated Infra Playbook — GPU Fleet, Capacity, Networking, IaC Modules, CI/CD, and Runbooks
author: Maya Thompson
content:
Summary

This integrated playbook codifies the operational patterns and IaC primitives we use to run Redwood's GPU fleet and associated infra: cloud accounts & networking, Terraform modules, CI/CD for runtime builds, and runbooks for common production incidents. It is a single reference for capacity planners, infra engineers, on-call SREs, and platform owners.

Goals and scope
- Ensure predictable capacity and predictable performance for inference workloads.
- Provide repeatable Terraform modules and CI pipeline patterns for provisioning GPU pools, VPCs, and networking.
- Define runbook actions for common incidents (high GPU utilization, OOMs, pod crashes, network egress / route flaps).
- Explain operational ownership and escalation paths.

Quick architecture overview
- GPU fleet: managed as regional nodepools backed by dedicated GPU instance groups (cloud-managed autoscaling disabled in most regions; we use horizontal pool autoscalers implemented in the control plane).
- Networking: each customer region has a shared VPC (redwood-core-vpc-<region>) and dedicated subnets for inference, control-plane, and monitoring. Cross-region traffic is controlled via transit gateways and egress NAT gateways for telemetry.
- IaC: all infra is provisioned via Terraform modules maintained under git::ssh://git.company/x/infra-modules (modules/gpu-pool, modules/vpc, modules/nat, modules/iam, modules/monitoring).
- CI/CD: pipelines build runtime containers, run end-to-end smoke tests against a canary cluster, and publish artifacts to the private registry. We use Jenkins for long-running flows and GitHub Actions for PR validations.

Ownership and SLAs
- Ownership: infra-engineering (gpu-infra subteam) owns GPU fleet modules and capacity; eng-sre owns runbooks and SLO enforcement; eng-platform owns CI/CD pipelines.
- SLOs and targets: average token latency (p50) < 120ms; availability SLO for inference pools 99.95% (regional); queue length target < 5 requests per GPU under steady state.

GPU capacity model (end-to-end)
1) Inputs collected weekly by capacity planners:
   - Peak RPS per region (30-day P95)
   - Average tokens per request & tokens/sec per model family
   - Target headroom (default 25%) for burst tolerance
2) Compute sizing formula (simplified):
   required_gpus = ceil((peak_rps * avg_tokens_per_request * avg_gflops_per_token) / (gpu_gflops_per_sec * seconds_per_rolling_window)) * (1 + headroom)
   Notes: we maintain a lookup table for tokens/sec per model and effective throughput for each instance SKU.
3) Batching and KV cache savings: subtract expected cache hit token savings before final allocation. Documented in the capacity workbook (link in related_pages).

Practical capacity run cadence
- Weekly: ingest telemetry dashboard, update 7/30/90 day trending, and run the capacity model spreadsheet.
- Monthly: reserve or release committed capacity, tag assets for billing.
- Pre-release (major model rollout): schedule a dry-run stress test on a pre-prod GPU pool 7 days prior.

Terraform / IaC module patterns
- Module boundaries: core modules per folder: modules/vpc, modules/subnet, modules/gpu-pool, modules/instance-profile, modules/iam, modules/monitoring, modules/dns. Keep modules small and composable.
- Example module usage (recommended pattern):

  ```hcl
  module "gpu_pool_inference" {
    source = "git::ssh://git.company/x/infra-modules.git//modules/gpu-pool?ref=v2026-08"
    region = "us-west-2"
    pool_name = "inference-a"
    instance_type = "nvidia-a100-80gb"
    min_size = 4
    desired_size = 32
    max_size = 64
    subnet_ids = module.vpc.inference_subnet_ids
    tags = { team = "gpu-infra", env = "prod" }
  }
  ```

- Common variables and outputs: every gpu-pool module must expose outputs: pool_id, instance_group_ids (list), sg_id, autoscaler_policy_id. Use these outputs when wiring monitoring/alerting.

Secrets and IAM patterns
- Use KMS-backed secrets for instance bootstrap keys.
- IAM roles: least-privilege policies scoped to pool / region; instance profiles only get retrieval access to model artifacts in the internal model-artifacts bucket.

Networking & cloud accounts
- Networking conventions:
  - VPC naming: redwood-core-vpc-<region>
  - Subnets: inference-private-<zone>, controlplane-private-<zone>, monitoring-private-<zone>
  - Security groups: sg-inference-<env> allow inbound from controlplane SG on ports 22, 9090 (prometheus) and 443 for control-plane API.
- Egress: telemetry egress flows through nat-telemetry-gw and is whitelisted per vendor.
- Cross-account: we use VPC peering for low-latency intra-region connections; cross-account route tables must be reviewed by cloud-accounts team.

CI/CD and build orchestration
- Pipeline stages (high level):
  1) PR validation: terraform fmt/lint, module unit tests (terraform-compliance), static analysis.
  2) Build: containerize runtime images via Jenkins X builder; cache layers are preserved in registry.
  3) Smoke: deploy to canary pool (tagged env=canary) and run smoke-suite (latency checks, correctness).
  4) Canary hold & manual approval: 1 hour automated tests + 10-minute manual review.
  5) Rollout: phased increase (10% -> 25% -> 100%) with automated rollback on error thresholds.
- Example GitHub Actions job for module tests (PRs):
  ```yaml
  name: TF-PR-Check
  on: [pull_request]
  jobs:
    fmt:
      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
      steps:
        - uses: actions/checkout@v3
        - name: Terraform fmt
          run: terraform fmt -check
        - name: Run tflint
          run: tflint
  ```

Release and rollback policy
- Rollouts use feature/traffic routing at the control plane and a rollout controller that shifts traffic. If p50 latency increases > 30% or error rate > 0.5% for 5 minutes, we automatically rollback to previous model variant and page oncall.

Monitoring, dashboards and alerts
- Dashboards: gpu-pool overview (grafana id: gpu-pool-overview-02), per-pool latency & queue length, GPU utilization heatmap.
- Alerts (examples):
  - GPU_UTIL_HIGH: fires at avg GPU util > 92% for 3m -> Slack #oncall-inf, PagerDuty P1.
  - GPU_OOM_RATE: container OOM rate > 0.5% in 5m -> PagerDuty P1 and runbook.
  - QUEUE_WAIT_HIGH: average queue depth > 8 requests/GPU for 2m -> P2, triggers autoscaler check.

Runbooks (playbook excerpts)
1) High GPU Utilization (avg > 92%)
   1. Confirm alert in Grafana and check affected pools (gpu-pool-overview-02).
   2. Run: kubectl -n inference get pods -o wide --selector=pool=<pool_name> and identify slow pods.
   3. If utilization persists and latency is rising: scale pool by +25% via Terraform plan/apply (change desired_size), or trigger preapproved burst capacity (see 'burst-capacity' runbook).
   4. If autoscaler misbehaving, disable autoscaler and scale manually, and file an incident.
   5. Post-incident: add capacity margin or adjust batching parameters.

2) OOMs / Pod CrashLoopBackOff
   1. Inspect pod logs: kubectl -n inference logs <pod>
   2. Check model size / quantization version mismatch with node SKU.
   3. If it's a model artifact mismatch, revert model variant via control plane and redeploy.
   4. If memory fragmentation suspected, rotate nodes: cordon -> drain -> replace (follow infra-engineering node rotation doc).

3) Network Egress Failures (monitoring down / telemetry missing)
   1. Verify NAT gateway state and route tables (cloud console or terraform state).
   2. Check VPC flow logs for blackholing.
   3. If cross-account route change detected, restore last-known-good route table from git history and roll forward a patch.

Operational notes and best practices
- Break large TF changes into small, reviewable modules; prefer plan-only PRs and stage apply via a dedicated pipeline user.
- Maintain a small set of approved instance SKUs for production (listed in modules/sku-allowlist.md).
- Keep per-pool throttles and request quotas in control plane to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
- Validate networking changes in a sandbox region before prod.

Run cadence and playbook maintenance
- This playbook is reviewed quarterly by gpu-infra and eng-sre. Major updates (new SKUs, model architecture changes) must trigger a playbook review and a dry-run test.

Appendix: Useful commands and snippets
- Terraform plan for gpu pool: terraform plan -var-file=env/prod.tfvars -target=module.gpu_pool_inference
- Promote a canary image: curl -X POST https://controlplane.redwood.internal/api/v1/rollouts -d '{"pool":"inference-a","image":"rg.redwood/internal/runtime:2026-11-01-canary"}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'

Contacts and escalation
- Primary: gpu-infra (oncall) -> PagerDuty: infra-gpu-primary (devops rotation).
- Secondary: eng-sre (oncall) -> PagerDuty: eng-sre-rotation.
- Pager and Slack: #oncall-infra, #infra-ops (for postmortem coordination).
